title: Core Primitives: Compute & Storage
summary: The building-block resource types every cloud service is composed from, independent of any one provider's product names.

slides.markdown:
Strip away any provider's branding and every cloud service is built from the same handful of primitives: **compute** (VMs, in various pricing flavors) and **storage** (object, block, file — each shaped for a different access pattern).

Knowing these primitives — not the provider-specific product names — is what lets you reason about any cloud, and is exactly what interviewers probe for.

slides.subTitle: Instance families and vCPU-to-memory ratio
slides.markdown:
A VM is sized by an **instance family**, each tuned for a workload shape: general-purpose (balanced vCPU:memory, e.g. 1:4), compute-optimized (more vCPU per GB, for CPU-bound work like encoding), and memory-optimized (more GB per vCPU, for in-memory caches or large databases).

The **vCPU-to-memory ratio** tells you what the instance is *for* at a glance — a 1:8 ratio screams "cache or database," a 1:2 ratio screams "batch compute." Picking the wrong family means paying for memory you don't use, or starving on the memory you actually need.

| | On-demand | Reserved | Spot/preemptible |
|---|---|---|---|
| Price | Highest, pay-as-you-go | Lower, in exchange for a 1-3 year commitment | Lowest — a discount on unused capacity |
| Can be interrupted? | No | No | Yes, with little to no warning |
| Best for | Unpredictable, short-term needs | Steady, known baseline load | Fault-tolerant, interruptible batch work |

**How to decide:** commit (reserved) for the load you know you'll always run, use spot for anything that can checkpoint and resume, and keep on-demand for the unpredictable remainder.

slides.subTitle: What each is for
slides.markdown:
| | Object storage | Block storage | File storage |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unit | Whole objects, accessed via HTTP API | Fixed-size blocks, attached to one VM | Files in a shared directory tree |
| Access | Any number of clients, over the network | One VM at a time (usually) | Many clients, POSIX-like |
| Example use | Photos, backups, static assets | A database's data volume | Shared config, home directories across VMs |

Each shape matches a different access pattern — object storage doesn't care about file hierarchies, block storage is fast but tied to one machine, and file storage trades some speed for shared, path-based access.

slides.subTitle: "11 nines" vs "99.99% uptime"
slides.markdown:
**Durability** measures whether your data *survives* over time — "11 nines" (99.999999999%) means the odds of losing an object in a year are vanishingly small, usually achieved by storing multiple copies across AZs. **Availability** measures whether the data is *reachable right now* — 99.99% availability still allows roughly 52 minutes of downtime a year.

A storage service can have extreme durability (your data is never lost) while still being briefly unavailable (you can't fetch it for a few minutes) — the two numbers answer different questions.

slides.subTitle: Hot, cool, cold/archive
slides.markdown:
Object storage is usually split into tiers by **access frequency, not by durability**: **hot** for data read constantly (higher storage cost, cheap/fast retrieval), **cool** for infrequent access (cheaper storage, small retrieval fee), and **cold/archive** for rarely-touched data (cheapest storage, slow retrieval — sometimes hours).

Lifecycle policies automatically move objects down the tiers as they age — a log file might live hot for a week, cool for a month, then archive for years of compliance retention, all without you touching it again.

slides.subTitle: Storage for a photo-sharing app
slides.markdown:
A photo-sharing app has three distinct data shapes, and each maps to a different primitive: the **uploaded photos themselves** go in object storage (huge volume, read from anywhere, never edited in place); the **user/post metadata database** sits on block storage attached to its DB instance (needs fast, consistent random I/O); and **shared application logs** written by multiple app servers go on file storage so every instance can append to the same log path.

Using one primitive for all three would either be slow, expensive, or both.

**Wrong belief:** "Block storage is faster, so I should use it for everything, including user file uploads."

**Why it's wrong:** block storage ties to a single VM and doesn't scale to millions of files accessed by arbitrary clients — you'd have to hand-build sharding and access yourself. Object storage is built for exactly that pattern, with near-unlimited scale and multi-client access baked in.

**Correct model:** block storage wins for low-latency, single-machine I/O (databases); object storage wins for large-scale, multi-client data (uploads, backups, assets).

slides.subTitle: VM to attached disk vs to object storage
slides.markdown:
The same VM talks to block storage and object storage very differently under the hood.

![A request's path from a VM to attached disk versus to object storage](assets/vm-storage-paths.svg)

Block storage is a dedicated, low-latency attachment — the OS sees it as just another disk. Object storage is reached over the network via an HTTP API call, no filesystem in between — why it scales to any number of clients but adds per-request latency.
